memo.thesis_en: A packaged-food company is a business I can explain in two paragraphs, and the numbers in front of me look attractive: a 5-year average ROE of 25.3%, a debt-to-equity of 0.07, and a price of $34.29 against a model intrinsic value of $72.42. But a 52.6% discount on a brand I'd call a good, not great, franchise makes me ask what the market sees that I don't. I can't verify ten years of earnings, management tenure, or the debt picture from this snapshot, and a debt-to-equity that low looks odd to me for a food company, so I won't treat it as established. Until I've checked those, I'll keep my hands in my pockets and put this on the watch list rather than buy on the fields that happen to be present.

The key questions are whether the brands retain pricing power against private label and whether management allocates capital sensibly. This snapshot does not answer them.

memo.thesis_en: Accenture screens well on the numbers I was given: a five-year average ROE of 27.7%, debt-to-equity of 0.003, and a computed margin of safety of 32.6% against an intrinsic value of $382.89 per share. But the snapshot gives me nothing about the business itself, so I cannot verify that the moat is durable. The question I keep asking is whether AI and automation will make this kind of consulting and outsourcing work cheaper to deliver and harder to charge for. A 5% discount rate and 8% growth rate also do much of the work in that valuation, and I would want to test it more conservatively. I will not write a check on a good-looking spreadsheet alone, so I watch and wait until I can check the earnings history, the moat evidence and management.

What I cannot check is whether the brand is fashion-driven and must be rebuilt every season. Nothing here shows 10 years of positive earnings, pricing power, retention, or management quality. So I am not buying yet. I will wait until I can answer those questions, because a wide margin of safety on an unchecked moat is not a margin of safety at all.

memo.thesis_en: I understand the business: Best Buy sells other people's electronics to consumers. That is where my trouble starts. I can't point to a moat here. It resells products it doesn't make, in a category where customers can compare prices in seconds, and the products themselves change fast. The numbers in front of me look respectable: a 48.4% five-year average ROE, a debt-to-equity of 0.39, and an 18.9% discount to a zero-growth owner-earnings value. But a cheap price on a business without a durable franchise is the cigar-butt mistake I made with Berkshire's textile mill. I'll pass and wait for a better pitch.
